extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and readers of political philosophy and legal theory (readers of Hobbes' Leviathan); policymakers interested in doctrine of sovereignty
extracted.subtask_description: An excerpt from Hobbes' Leviathan setting out criteria for what counts as punishment (vs hostility), enumerating types of punishments and rewards, and listing doctrines and institutional defects that weaken or dissolve a commonwealth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Origin of the Sovereign's Right to Punish
rubrics_metrics.description: The Right which the Common-wealth (i.e., he, or they that represent it) hath to Punish, is not grounded on any concession, or gift of the Subjects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sovereign punishment springs from the original natural right (each man having had a right to everything before commonwealth) which, when subjects lay down their rights, strengthens the sovereign's own pre-existing right. It was not 'given' by subjects but left in the sovereign as entire (subject only to limits set by natural law).

rubrics_metrics.name: Private Injuries and Revenges Are Not Punishments
rubrics_metrics.description: Neither private revenges, nor injuries of private men, can properly be styled Punishment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because they do not proceed from public authority; punishment, by definition, must be inflicted by public (sovereign) authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Denial of Preferment Is Not Punishment
rubrics_metrics.description: To be neglected, and unpreferred by the publique favour, is not a Punishment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Neglect or failure to prefer someone inflicts no new evil; the person remains in their prior estate, so this does not meet the definition of punishment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pain Inflicted Without Public Hearing Is Not Punishment
rubrics_metrics.description: The evill inflicted by publique Authority, without precedent publique condemnation, is not to be styled Punishment; but of an hostile act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Punishment requires that the fact be first judged by public authority to be a transgression of the law; punishment without prior public condemnation is hostility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pain Inflicted by Usurped Power Is Not Punishment
rubrics_metrics.description: The evill inflicted by usurped power, and Judges without Authority from the Soveraign, is not Punishment; but an act of hostility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acts by authorities lacking sovereign authorization have no legitimate claim to be 'punishment' because they do not flow from public/sovereign authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pain Inflicted Without Respect to Future Good Is Not Punishment
rubrics_metrics.description: All evill which is inflicted without intention, or possibility of disposing the Delinquent, or (by his example) other men, to obey the Lawes, is not Punishment; but an act of hostility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Punishment must aim to bring about future obedience (deterrence or reform). If inflicted without such an end, it is not punishment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural Evil Consequences Are Not Human Punishments
rubrics_metrics.description: Hurt that follows naturally from actions (e.g., being slain or wounded when assaulting another, or falling into sickness by unlawful act) is not contained in the name of Punishment in respect of men.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such harms may be 'divine' punishments from God or Nature, but not punishments imposed by human public authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hurt Less Than the Benefit of Transgressing Is Not Punishment
rubrics_metrics.description: If the harm inflicted be less than the benefit, or contentment that naturally followeth the crime committed, that harm is not within the definition [of punishment]; and is rather the Price, or Redemption, than the Punishment of a Crime.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because punishment's purpose is to dispose people to obey law; if penalty is too small relative to gain it will not deter and thus is not a true punishment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Excessive Hurt Beyond Legal Penalty Is Hostility, Not Punishment
rubrics_metrics.description: If a Punishment be determined and prescribed in the Law itself, and after the crime committed, there be a greater Punishment inflicted, the excesse is not Punishment, but an act of hostility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The declared lesser penalty eliminates the terror of an unknown greater one; unexpected additions are not part of legitimate punishment. Where no penalty is prescribed, arbitrary punishment may be considered punishment (because offender expects indeterminate punishment).

rubrics_metrics.name: Harm Inflicted for Acts Before a Law Existed Is Not Punishment
rubrics_metrics.description: Harm inflicted for a Fact done before there was a Law that forbad it, is not Punishment, but an act of Hostility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Punishment presupposes a judged transgression of a law; without a law at the time of the act there can be no legal punishment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hurt Inflicted on the Representative Is Not Punishment
rubrics_metrics.description: Hurt inflicted on the Representative of the Common-wealth, is not Punishment, but an act of Hostility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because public authority to punish resides only in the representative itself; one cannot punish the representative by ordinary punishment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harm to Revolted Subjects Is Right of War, Not Punishment
rubrics_metrics.description: Harm inflicted upon one that is a declared enemy, falls not under the name of Punishment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Declared enemies (those who deny subjection) are treated by the commonwealth as enemies and may lawfully be made to suffer according to the will of the representative; the punishments in law are directed to subjects, not enemies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division of Punishments: Divine and Humane
rubrics_metrics.description: Punishments are first distributed into Divine, and Humane.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Divine punishments (to be discussed elsewhere) are from God; humane are those inflicted by command of man and subdivided into corporal, pecuniary, ignominy, imprisonment, exile, or mixed forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corporal Punishment
rubrics_metrics.description: Corporal Punishment is that which is inflicted on the body directly, and according to the intention of him that inflicteth it: such as are stripes, or wounds, or deprivation of such pleasures of the body.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Corporal punishment targets bodily harms or the deprivation of bodily pleasures previously lawfully enjoyed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capital vs Less-than-Capital Distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitall is the Infliction of Death; Less than Capitall are Stripes, Wounds, Chains, and any other corporall Paine, not in its own nature mortall.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If death is not intended by the inflicter it is not properly capital even if death accidentally results; capital requires intention or direct infliction of death.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pecuniary Punishment
rubrics_metrics.description: Pecuniary Punishment consists in the deprivation of a Summe of Mony, but also of Lands, or any other goods usually bought and sold for mony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a law is designed to gather money as a price for privilege or exemption, it is not properly punishment but a price for dispensation—except where the law is natural or religious (then the mulct is punishment). Restitution to injured parties is satisfaction extinguishing the private accusation but not necessarily the crime.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ignominy
rubrics_metrics.description: Ignominy is the infliction of such Evill, as is made Dishonorable; or the deprivation of such Good, as is made Honourable by the Common-wealth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Natural honors (courage, wisdom) cannot be taken by law and so their loss is not punishment; honors created by the commonwealth (titles, badges, offices) can be taken away and are proper punishments (e.g., degrading a condemned man's badges, titles, offices).

rubrics_metrics.name: Imprisonment
rubrics_metrics.description: Imprisonment is when a man is by publique Authority deprived of liberty; and may happen from two divers ends: (1) safe custody of an accused, (2) inflicting pain on a condemned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Custodial restraint before hearing beyond that necessary for custody is not punishment and violates natural law; imprisonment as punishment follows after judicial conviction. Imprisonment includes confinement to prison, islands, forced labor (quarries, galleys), chains, or other external impediments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exile (Banishment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Exile is when a man is for a crime, condemned to depart out of the dominion of the Common-wealth ... and during a prefixed time, or for ever, not to return into it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In itself exile may not be a punishment but an escape or public command to avoid punishment by flight; if the banished retains goods/revenue, mere change of air is not punishment. When combined with deprivation of lands/goods the punishment is pecuniary rather than the exile itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punishment of the Innocent Is Contrary to the Law of Nature
rubrics_metrics.description: All Punishments of Innocent subjects, be they great or little, are against the Law of Nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Three reasons: (1) punishment is aimed at future public good — punishing innocents yields no public good; (2) it is ingratitude versus the sovereign who protects the obedient; (3) it violates equity (equal distribution of justice).

rubrics_metrics.name: Harms to Innocents in War May Be Lawful
rubrics_metrics.description: The Infliction of what evill soever, on an Innocent man, that is not a Subject, if it be for the benefit of the Common-wealth, and without violation of any former Covenant, is no breach of the Law of Nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Non-subjects are either enemies or no-longer-subjects; against enemies the original right of nature to make war applies and the victor need not distinguish between innocent and guilty as pertains to past acts; rebels who renounce subjection suffer as enemies (vengeance may extend even to later generations in consequence).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reward: Salary vs Grace
rubrics_metrics.description: REWARD is either of Gift, or by Contract. When by Contract, it is called Salary, and Wages; when of Gift, it is benefit proceeding from the Grace of them that bestow it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Salary (contractual reward) makes the recipient bound in justice to perform the office; gifts (grace) create obligations of honor or gratitude but not enforceable legal duty. Common soldiers may claim wages as debt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Benefits Bestowed for Fear Are Not Rewards
rubrics_metrics.description: Benefits which a Soveraign bestoweth on a Subject, for fear of some power, and ability he hath to do hurt to the Common-wealth, are not properly Rewards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: They are extorted by fear (sacrifices) and do not encourage obedience but rather extortion and further demands; they are neither salary nor grace in the proper sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Certain vs Casual Salaries and Their Effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Some Salaries are certain, proceeding from the publique Treasure; others uncertain and casual, proceeding from the execution of the Office for which the Salary is ordained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Casual/uncertain salaries in judicature are harmful: they nourish suits (more suits yield more benefit) and encourage jurisdictional competition; offices of execution are less susceptible to these problems because their employment cannot be increased by the officeholder's efforts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dissolution from Imperfect Institution
rubrics_metrics.description: Dissolution of Common-wealths proceedeth from Imperfect Institution and resemble diseases of a natural body which proceed from defectuous procreation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If founders lack the art of framing firm lasting laws or the humility/patience to govern, commonwealths will be ill-formed and vulnerable to internal disorder and eventual collapse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Want of Absolute Power
rubrics_metrics.description: That a man to obtain a Kingdome, is sometimes content with lesse Power, than to the Peace, and defence of the Common-wealth is necessarily required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When sovereigns deny themselves necessary powers (often to recover them later), the gap invites internal rebellion and foreign interference; insufficiently absolute power at foundation predisposes to dissolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Private Judgment of Good and Evil Weakens Commonwealth
rubrics_metrics.description: The doctrine that every private man is Judge of Good and Evill actions disposes men to debate and dispute commands of the commonwealth and to obey or disobey at will.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The measure of good and evil under civil society is the civil law and the legislator as representative; private judging fragments obedience and weakens the commonwealth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Erroneous Conscience Is Not a Safe Rule Under Civil Law
rubrics_metrics.description: The doctrine that whatsoever a man does against his Conscience is Sin is repugnant to civil society because conscience and judgement may be erroneous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under civil law the public law is the public conscience; private consciences are diverse private opinions that would distract the commonwealth if taken as authoritative in law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pretence of Inspiration Undermines Civil Authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Teaching that Faith and Sanctity are attained by supernatural inspiration rather than study and reason leads men to claim no need to render reasons and to prefer personal inspiration to the law of the country.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This pretence makes private men into judges of good and evil and can dissolve civil government; faith and sanctity are better explained as results of education, discipline, and natural means.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sovereign Subject to Civil Laws Is a Dangerous Doctrine
rubrics_metrics.description: The doctrine that he that hath the Soveraign Power, is subject to the Civill Lawes is repugnant to the nature of a Common-wealth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sovereigns are subject only to the laws of nature; making the sovereign subject to civil laws would set a judge above him and create competing sovereigns, leading to confusion and dissolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attributing Absolute Propriety to Subjects Undermines Sovereignty
rubrics_metrics.description: The doctrine that every private man has an absolute Propriety in his Goods excluding the Right of the Soveraign tends to the dissolution of a Common-wealth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each man has property excluding other subjects but that property derives from the sovereign's protection; excluding sovereign rights prevents the sovereign from performing duties of defence and justice, so commonwealth cannot function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dividing the Sovereign Power Destroys the Commonwealth
rubrics_metrics.description: The doctrine that the Soveraign Power may be divided is plainly and directly against the essence of a Common-wealth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dividing power mutual destroys it; multiple sovereigns means multiple commonwealths in one body politic, producing faction and dissolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitation of Neighbour Nations Can Cause Instability
rubrics_metrics.description: The example of different government in a neighbouring Nation disposeth men to alteration of the forme already settled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seeing neighbors enriched by different constitutions tempts imitation and dangerous change; proximity and envy can provoke sedition and disorder.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reading Ancient Histories (Greeks and Romans) May Encourage Rebellion
rubrics_metrics.description: Reading books of policy and histories of the antient Greeks and Romans gives young men a pleasing idea of popular government and may tempt them to kill kings or call them tyrants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ancient accounts often omit the seditions and civil wars that produced those regimes' instability; without proper correction they poison minds ('biting of a mad Dogge') and create 'tyrannophobia' or appetite for novelty leading to rebellion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ghostly Authority Versus Civil Authority Causes Dual Sovereignty
rubrics_metrics.description: Setting up Supremacy (spiritual) against Soveraignty (temporal) produces two Kingdomes of the same Subjects and risks civil war and dissolution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If spiritual and civil powers both claim supreme authority (e.g., to declare what is sin or law), subjects face two masters; the resulting conflict suffocates the commonwealth, like an epileptic seizure in a body.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mixt Government Creates Multiple Sovereigns and Factions
rubrics_metrics.description: When different sovereign faculties (levying money, command, making laws) are placed in separate assemblies or persons, the commonwealth is divided into factions rather than being one independent sovereign.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such a mixed arrangement produces lack of nourishment (revenue), lack of motion (command), or lack of rational lawmaking; practically it is three independent factions and three sovereigns, which cannot stand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Want of Money Weakens the Commonwealth
rubrics_metrics.description: Difficulty of raising money for necessary uses of the commonwealth, especially in war, is a disease arising from subjects' opinion that they have absolute property excluding sovereign rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If sovereign cannot access funds due to subjects' tenacity, it will resort to legal stratagems or violent measures to obtain supplies; repeated extremes may bring the people to due temper or lead to the commonwealth's ruin.
